titleStmt.title: Underprovisioned GPUs: On Sufficient Capacity for Real-Time Mission-Critical Perception

analytic.title: Underprovisioned GPUs: On Sufficient Capacity for Real-Time Mission-Critical Perception

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Recent work suggests that computing resources, such as GPUs in real-time edge-based perception systems, need not have sufficient capacity to keep up with the input frame rates of all input devices (e.g., cameras) at their full-frame resolution. Rather, they can be under-provisioned because only parts of any given frame need to be inspected (i.e., paid attention to). This paper derives an attention allocation policy, called canvas-based attention scheduling that decides which parts of each frame of each device to inspect, and a corresponding schedulability condition that relates the spatiotemporal properties of surrounding objects to the ability of the edge-based perception subsystem to keep up with the state of the environment in real-time. It provides a quantitative estimate of adequate computing capacity for the expected perception workload. We implement a canvasbased attention scheduler for an object detection application and perform an empirical comparative study based on actual GPU hardware and surveillance videos. Results show that canvas-based attention scheduling keeps up with the environment while using a much smaller GPU capacity, compared with prior approaches.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: According to a recent market study 1 , video surveillance applications are predicted to reach 30% of the global Edge-AI market that is expected to grow from just under $6 Billion USD today to over $39 billion USD by 2032. The report further says that "the rising demand for edge AI is due to the increasing real-time processing of data and [need for] accuracy". The predicted growth of the video surveillance segment of the edge AI market, together with its need for real-time accurate processing, leads to the question addressed in this paper: in a typical edge-based surveillance application, how to reduce the workload on the edge server that implements the needed analytics on input streams?

Consider a server that is fed multiple input data streams in real-time from surrounding surveillance devices (e.g., cameras). How much capacity is needed to keep up with the input streams? A trivial answer is that the server should be fast enough to keep up with the aggregate frame rate from all the input devices at their full-frame resolution. Recent work, however, shows that the capacity needed is much lower [1]- [5] because not all parts of all frames need to be inspected by the server's analytics. For example, static backgrounds are redundant and need not be inspected in every frame. Similarly, slowly moving objects can be inspected at a lower frequency than faster objects. This paper derives a tight capacity (also known in realtime literature as schedulability) condition for a mode of real-time perceptual input processing we call canvas-based attention scheduling. In this mode, the capacity of the perception pipeline is less than what's needed to process the multidimensional input data streams received from all the input devices at their original frame rate. Instead, patches of interest in those frames are consolidated into a space (called the canvas) that is smaller than the sum of all input device data rates. The server needs only to keep up with the canvas frame rate at the canvas frame resolution and not with the original overall frame rate at the original resolution.

Different patches (containing objects of interest in the environment) are inspected by the perception subsystem at different frequencies. For example, slower and more predictable objects may be inspected less frequently than faster and less predictable ones. This multi-frequency observation technique is inspired by the target tracking in phased-array radars [6], where different targets may be illuminated (inspected) by the radar at different rates, depending on their current maneuvers and speed. An example implementation of this multi-frequency inspection scheme in practice (in the context of autonomous perceptions systems) was described in recent work [1]. It uses optical flow [7] to update the location of foreground objects in the scene, then chooses which of these foreground patches to inspect by the perception subsystem at which rate.

Canvas-based attention scheduling with multi-frequency object inspection improves the efficiency and timeliness of machine perception subsystems of modern autonomous systems, such as autonomous surveillance, self-driving cars, drones, and aided target recognition (AiTR/defense) systems. It gives rise to a novel scheduling problem, where (patches containing) different objects are mapped to different quasi-periodic inspection tasks 2 that need to be served once per period in order to satisfy their respective inspection deadlines. In this paper, we apply this problem to the processing of video frames, derive a schedulability bound for the resulting canvas-based attention scheduler, and empirically evaluate the scheduler using video traces from real surveillance cameras. The problem is, in a sense, a generalization of the way humans allocate their cognitive capacity. For example, when watching a movie, rather than allocating equal attention to each screen pixel, humans allocate it only to some parts of the screen where the "action" is. The canvas abstraction is a stylized representation of such region(s) of attention.

Our schedulability bound is novel in relating the spatial properties of objects in the original input frames to the ability of the canvas-based attention scheduler to meet all inspection deadlines. It allows choosing the right processing capacity for the perception subsystem, given expected object characteristics in the perceived environment, such that no inspection deadlines are missed. The bound is spatio-temporal in nature because it simultaneously reflects spatial (bin-packing-like canvas size) constraints and temporal (inspection deadline) constraints.

We argue that spatiotemporal scheduling and schedulability analysis problems, exemplified by the one formulated in this paper, are an emerging frontier of growing importance for real-time scheduling research. This is because the increasingly data-intensive processing pipelines of modern AI-driven cyberphysical applications call for mechanisms that fit data into spatial templates (such as neural network input templates) with size limits, while requiring that the data be processed within time limits, resulting in feasibility analysis challenges that feature both spatial and temporal constraints. While scheduling problems with both time and capacity constraints are plentiful in past literature, what's new is that spatial relations between pixels of each data item must be preserved in all input dimensions for the AI algorithm to recognize the item, making the multidimensional item packing problem (into the canvas), subject to size and deadline constraints, harder compared to, say, serializing data bits for transmission over a network link under deadline and capacity constraints.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the execution model and develops the scheduling problem statement. Section III presents describes the schedulability condition, and offers a basic proof. Section IV describes system implementation details. Section V evaluates a real implementation of this system using a surveillance camera dataset. Related work is summarized in Section VI. Section VII discusses limitations and opportunities for future work. The paper concludes with Section VIII.

div.head: II. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: The spatiotemporal scheduling problem addressed in this paper arises in intelligent systems, such as robots, drones, and intelligent security cameras, that utilize (i) complex sensors such as cameras, infrared imaging sensors, or LiDARs to capture objects in their environment (e.g., in pictures or 3D point clouds), and (ii) a downstream AI-based perception module that interprets the sensor data in real-time. Sensors in such systems produce multi-dimensional data frames. These frames are processed by the perception subsystem to create a structured representation of the external world. If we choose a processing capacity that is smaller than what is needed to process the original input size from all sensors at the original frame rate, and instead process different parts of the input at different frequencies commensurate with their state volatility, an interesting schedulability problem arises. Below, we formulate this schedulability problem. Description of practical implementation details is delegated to the implementation section (Section IV).

div.head: A. The Execution Model
div.p: Consider a set S of sensors, such as cameras or LiDARs. Each sensor s ∈ S generates a time series, F s , of multidimensional data frames produced at frame rate, r. For notational simplicity, we assume that the rate is the same for all sensors, but this limitation can be removed, since what matters is the total data rate, not how it is divided across individual sensors. We adopt a discrete-time model, where time k refers to the arrival time of the k th frame in F s . Let this frame be denoted by F s k . Let the number of dimensions (for the frame) be denoted by d. For example, a camera would generate a series of two-dimensional images (d = 2), whereas a LiDAR might generate a series of three-dimensional point clouds (d = 3). Let V s denote the size (i.e., area, if d = 2, or volume, if d = 3) of frame F s k . Let V denote the combined total volume V = s∈S V s of all sensor frames arriving at each time step, k. The perception module comprises a processing element (in our implementation, a GPU) that is provisioned to process (at frame rate r) an input of volume at most V GP U , where V GP U < V . We call this smaller volume the canvas frame. Let the k th canvas frame be denoted, C k .

The external world features a set of objects of interest, O, where each object, O i ∈ O, enters and leaves the field of view of some sensor s in frames F s ai and F s fi , respectively. Times a i and f i are not known a priori. We are not concerned with object re-identification. Thus, if an object reappears later in the same or another sensor's view, it can be thought of as a new object. We further assume that the sensors have nonoverlapping views in order to maximize coverage. If sensor views overlap, the sensors can divide the areas of overlap among themselves (for monitoring and reporting purposes) as described in prior work [8].

Let set O(k) comprise all objects, O i , that are within some sensor's field of view at time k (i.e., for which a i ≤ k < f i ). Each object O i ∈ O(k) is associated with a quasi-periodic inspection task, τ i , with an implicit deadline model. The first invocation of this task arrives at time a i (i.e., when the object first enters the field of view of some sensor, s). A new invocation of this task arrives at the expiration time (deadline) of the previous invocation. The arrival of a new invocation of the inspection task, τ i , means that the object O i is selected for inspection from the current input frame, say F s k . Inspection of this object by the perception module must then occur within an interval, D k i , called the inspection interval. Otherwise, an inspection deadline is said to be missed. More specifically, a selected object, O i , from frame F s k must be included for processing in some canvas frame, C k+m , such that 0 ≤ m ≤ D k i (thus completing the execution of the said inspection task invocation before the next invocation arrives). The inspection task, τ i , for object O i is quasi-periodic in the sense that the next invocation of the task may be associated with a different inspection interval. For example, if the object gains speed, the inspection interval may be reduced. In general, D k i may depend on the type and mobility characteristics of the object. Faster and less predictably-moving objects may have a smaller D k i .

div.head: B. The Capacity Problem
div.p: The problem solved in this paper is to derive a condition under which the canvas-based attention scheduler at the edge server meets all real-time inspection deadlines (for a given canvas volume V GP U ). We assume that the server's GPU is the bottleneck resource. While sensors communicate with the server via a network, since the server is on the edge (not in the cloud), we do not consider network capacity as the bottleneck, especially with current advances in wireless and the possibility of having point-to-point wired connections to individual cameras in many surveillance applications.

The result in this paper can be used to decide on the best V GP U offline in a manner that allows the edge server to keep up with a set of hypothetical "benchmark traffic" scenarios (without missing deadlines), or indeed to decide online if the current set of visible objects can be inspected in time. If they can't, an alternative action can thus be taken, such as image resizing (downsizing) [9]. The scheduler operates as follows:

1) Each new object O i is selected by the attention scheduler as soon as it enters the field of view of some sensor, s (i.e., in frame F s ai ). 2) To ensure continuous monitoring, an object O i selected in frame F s k is selected again in frame F s k+D k i (until it exits the field of view of sensor s). 3) Every object O i selected from the input frame F s k must be processed within its inspection interval D k i . In other words, it must be included in some canvas frame C k+m , where 0 ≤ m < D k i . 4) All regions included in a canvas frame must fit (without overlap) within its volume, V GP U . The set of objects is said to be schedulable if a schedule exists that satisfies the above conditions. Below, we derive the schedulability condition.

div.head: III. AN EDF SCHEDULABILITY CONDITION
div.p: In practice, from analyzing the dimensions of a large number of objects related to surveillance and traffic scenarios (e.g., cars, people bicycles, etc), we found that patches of an aspect ratio of 1:1, 1:2, and 2:1 would be suitable to cover the majority of these objects. Thus, in the following, we derive schedulability conditions for the case where (i) the patches extracted from input frames are inserted in canvas frames in EDF order, according to their inspection deadlines, and (ii) these patches adhere to a finite set of predetermined sizes whose dimensions have the aforementioned aspect ratio. This size quantization facilitates packing them onto the canvas.

Specifically, we use equilateral canvas frames with sides of length, L (and thus, volume V GP U = L d ). Patches selected from the input frames are d-dimensional cuboids whose sides in each of the different dimensions divide L by some (possibly different) power of 2, such that any two sides can have an aspect ratio of either 1:1 or 1:2 (equivalently, 2:1). Objects that are too large to fit into any of the above-sized blocks are simply downsized to the largest allowable size. The rationale is that such objects, being so large, can be re-sized with relative impunity, in that the perception subsystem should still be able to recognize them.

div.head: A. Instantaneous Canvas Utilization
div.p: In this section, we define the notion of canvas utilization. Subsequent sections will derive schedulability conditions expressed in terms of this utilization. Consider a time, k, and a set of objects currently in the combined sensor field of view, O(k). For each object, O i ∈ O(k), let k i refer to the latest invocation time of the corresponding inspection task, τ i (meaning, k i is the index of the most recent input frame from which object O i ∈ O(k) was selected for inspection by the attention scheduler). Let v ki i be the volume of object O i in that frame. Let D ki i be the corresponding inspection interval. We define the instantaneous canvas utilization, U canvas (k) as follows:
div.formula: U canvas (k) = Oi∈O(k) v ki i /V GP U D ki i(1)

div.head: B. The Trivial Schedulability Condition
div.p: Clearly, no object can be bigger than the size of a canvas frame, or else it is unschedulable. In this section, we also trivially show that if the maximum object (or patch) size is not further bounded, inspection deadlines can still be missed at nearly zero canvas utilization. To see this by example, consider a set of two inspection tasks, where the first inspects a very small object, O 1 , of size v 1 ≈ 0 every frame (i.e., with D 1 = 1). The second inspects an object, O 2 , the size of an entire canvas frame (v 2 = V GP U ) and has a large inspection deadline (D 2 >> 1). Substituting in Equation ( 1), it is easy to see that at any time, k. the canvas utilization U canvas (k) ≈ 0.

Since each canvas frame is partially occupied with the first object, O 1 , there is never room for the second, and an inspection deadline is missed. In other words, in the absence of an appropriate bound on maximum object size, deadlines can be missed at near-zero canvas utilization.

To avoid the above pessimistic result, in the rest of the analysis, we assume that the largest object has size v max < V GP U , where v max is a configurable design parameter. In practice, this constraint can be easily enforced by object resizing. An object whose size exceeds the desired v max can be resized to v max with relative impunity (prior to placing it in the canvas) because such large objects will still be (very likely) recognized by the perception subsystem even after resizing.

div.head: C. An Upper Limit
div.p: Inspired by the reasoning behind multiprocessor utilization bounds, we now trivially prove the following theorem.
Theorem 1: The canvas utilization bound for schedulability under an EDF canvas-based attention scheduling policy cannot be higher than 1 -v max /V GP U .

Proof: To see that the theorem is true, consider a set of inspection tasks, each with an inspection period of 1 (i.e., D i = 1) and a collective object volume, i v i that is infinitesimally bigger than V GP U -v max (thus leaving just under v max in available space). An object of size v max then arrives that needs to be inspected within some large interval D >> 1. Since each canvas frame has less than v max in available space, the object does not fit in any of the canvas frames. Thus, an inspection deadline is missed. div.head: D. The Tight Schedulability Condition
div.p: In this section, we prove that the above bound is in fact tight. In other words, no deadlines are missed if canvas utilization does not exceed 1 -v max /V GP U . We express this result more formally as follows.
Theorem 2: A set of objects in the field of view at time k, denoted O(k), meets its inspection deadlines if:
div.formula: Oi∈O(k) v ki i /V GP U D ki i ≤ 1 - v max V GP U(2)
div.p: where k i is the last time the object was selected for inspection (i.e, the last invocation time of inspection task τ i ), v ki i is the object volume at time k i , and D ki i is the inspection deadline for this invocation.

Intuitively, to prove the theorem, we will show that if the inspection deadline of an object is missed, each canvas frame from the last invocation of the corresponding inspection task and until its deadline must be at least 1-v max /V GP U utilized.
To do so, we first describe our algorithm for packing objects into canvas frames and prove a property of that algorithm that we need for the schedulability result, then go back and prove the theorem.

div.head: E. The Recursive Consolidation Algorithm
div.p: Consider a set of objects to be inserted in the canvas, ordered in EDF fashion by their inspection deadlines. The consolidation algorithm packs these objects in successive canvas frames, starting with the current frame, say C k . Without loss of generality, we denote the indices of objects packed into canvas frame C k by i 1 , i 2 , ..., i M , in EDF order, where O i M is the first object that does not fit into C k (and is instead postponed until C k+1 ). The consolidation algorithm attempts to pack subsets, O i1 , O i2 , ..., O i l , of the above order list, starting with O i1 (i.e., l = 1), and increasing l until C k overflow.

To understand how the objects are packed, it is useful to conceive of a canvas frame as composed of nested containers. The entire canvas is a Level 1 container. Each subsequent level splits the previous level in half recursively along its largest dimension (ties broken arbitrarily). Thus, a Level i container is half the size of a Level i-1 container. For illustration, the relation between containers of five levels in a two-dimensional canvas is shown in Figure 1. Now consider packing objects O i1 , ..., O i l for some l ≥ 1. Since sizes are quantized, each object is put in a container exactly its size. Starting with the smallest container size, every two full Level i containers are then packed into one Level i-1 container, as shown in Figure 1. We say they are consolidated. Since successive levels differ by a factor of two in one dimension only, two Level i containers always fit exactly into one Level i-1 container. Consolidation is carried out recursively until no more consolidation is possible. We call it the recursive consolidation algorithm. It is easy to show the following lemma:
Lemma 1: The recursive consolidation algorithm leaves at most one partially full container at any level.
Proof: To see why the above lemma is true, we do an induction on object size, from the smallest possible size to the largest size.

The base case: First, consider the smallest object size, v min . There can be either an even or an odd number of objects of size v min . If the number is even (including zero), these objects can be perfectly consolidated into (half as many) containers of the next size up (possibly zero). Let us call them Level j containers. If the number is odd, exactly one partial container of Level j will be left. Thus, in any case, at most one Level j partially full container will be left.

The induction step: Now assume that objects of sizes up to v s have been consolidated into containers of the next size up. Let us call them Level j containers. Per induction invariant, assume there is only one partially full container of Level j . Let us call it partial container A. Now consider the object of the next size up. If there is an even number of them (including zero), they will fill a number of Level j-1 containers exactly. The one partial Level j container will give rise to the only partial Level j-1 container. If the number of objects is odd, however, then one of these objects can fit exactly a Level j container. Let us call it container B, while the rest will exactly fit a number of Level j-1 containers. Level j containers A and B can now be put together into a single partially full Level j-1 container. Thus, there will be at most one partially full Level j-1 container.

By induction, in any one canvas frame at most one container of any level can be partially full. Now, consider an object O i selected for inspection at some time k that ultimately misses its inspection deadline, D k i . This implies that frames C k , ..., C k+D k i -1 were filled with objects of earlier deadlines and did not have room for object O i . We call such a set of successive busy frames an EDF busy period.
Lemma 2: Within the EDF busy period, no canvas frame is packed with less than volume (V GP U -v max ) worth of objects.

Proof: Consider a canvas frame, C k , in the busy period. Since all objects are of size v max or less, clearly frame C k cannot have an empty container of that size, or else object O i could have been placed in that container and no deadline would have been missed. By Lemma 1, frame C k also cannot have more than one partially full container of size v max (the remaining containers of that size must be full). The total volume packed in each canvas frame C k in the busy period is thus at least
Next, we prove Theorem 2 which states that the attention scheduler meets all deadlines if for all k:
div.formula: Oi∈O(k) v ki i /V GP U D ki i ≤ 1 - v max V GP U
div.p: Proof of Theorem 2: Consider a hypothetical set of aperiodic tasks on a uniprocessor, where each task τ i needs a number of clock cycles, v ki i to finish, and has a deadline D ki i (expressed in units of time we call scheduler ticks). Imagine these tasks running on a uniprocessor of speed (V GP U -v max ) cycles per scheduler tick. Note that, since the perception subsystem will process at least data volume (V GP U -v max ) per canvas frame, and since tasks fill up canvas frames in EDF order, when compared on scheduler tick (canvas frame) boundaries any tasks that finished on the hypothetical uniprocessor will correspond to objects that have been processed by the perception subsystem. Thus, if the hypothetical uniprocessor is schedulable, so will the perception system.
The execution time, C i , of task τ i on the hypothetical uniprocessor is the number of cycles it needs, divided by the processor speed, or
div.formula: C i = v ki i /(V GP U -v max ).
div.p: The schedulability condition for independent aperiodic tasks on a uniprocessor using EDF is known to be:
div.formula: Oi∈O(k) C i D ki i ≤ 1(3)
div.p: Substituting for C i in the above equation and rearranging, we get that the uniprocessor task set is schedulable if:
div.formula: Oi∈O(k) v ki i /V GP U D ki i ≤ 1 - v max V GP U(4)
div.p: By the comparative argument made above, the above sufficient schedulability condition also applies to the original perception system as well.
From Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, we also conclude that the bound in Theorem 2 is tight.

div.head: IV. IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: We implement the canvas-based attention scheduling framework for an object detection application. In this section, we introduce the architecture of the system and several practical considerations for implementation.

The architecture of the implemented system is illustrated in Figure 2. For the input frames F s of each individual sensor s, we apply a background subtraction-based algorithm to detect the location of foreground objects. For more dynamic scenarios, background subtraction can be replaced with optical flow [1]. New object regions in the sensor's view are detected by comparing the predicted known object locations with the background subtraction results. If background subtraction indicates a new patch not corresponding to any of the predicted known object locations, a new object is assumed.

Since background subtraction detects motion only, when an object stops moving, it becomes a part of the background. To avoid losing the object, a memory module is implemented that remembers the last seen location of each object. An object is removed only when it moves out of the frame or its corresponding memorized region is inspected by the perception module and it verifies that the object is no longer present. When the system starts, it runs a full frame detection at the original resolution to locate all existing objects and uses these detection results as a starting point of the algorithm.

As a practical approximation, we set D k i to be inversely proportional to the detected speed of object O i in frame F s k . Specifically, the object speed is mapped to a finite set of inspection interval values ranging from 1 to 5 (corresponding to the object being processed every frame to at least being processed every 5 frames). We also define a maximum D i , so we continue to check on very slow or stopped objects. The idea is that regions of the screen that change more quickly need to be inspected more frequently.

Each object O i , detected by background subtraction in frame F s k , of sensor s, selected from input frame F s k occupies a region whose size is denoted by v k i , and is associated with an inspection interval, D k i , computed from the speed of the object according to optical flow. Let the end-point of object O i 's inspection interval be denoted by d k i . The scheduling algorithm at the server fills canvas frames in an earliest-deadline first manner according to d k i . At time index, k, the algorithm fills canvas frame C k first. Once full, the remaining objects are postponed until a future frame.

In order to opportunistically improve canvas utilization, we implement an enhancement on top of EDF. In the enhanced policy, the scheduler first fills the current canvas frame, following regular EDF. If the next object in EDF order does not fit in the current frame, the algorithm searches the queue of remaining objects and brings later objects into the current frame if they can fit in. This opportunistic advance improves the utilization of the current frame as much as possible, without negatively affecting the ability to meet deadlines.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of the canvas-based attention scheduling architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier platform with a realistic surveillance camera dataset and present the results.

A. Experiment Setup 1) Hardware Platform: we conduct all experiments on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier SoC, a widely used AI-powered embedded platform. The Jetson AGX Xavier features an 8core Carmel Arm v8.2 64-bit CPU, a 512-core Volta GPU, and 32 GB memory shared by both the CPU and the GPU. We set the power mode to MAXN and configure the GPU to run at a constant clock frequency.

2) Dataset: We use the VIRAT video surveillance dataset [10] for all of our experiments. Because this dataset is primarily designed for activity recognition, it only provides labels for objects involved in its target activity classes. To avoid this limitation, we use the Xlarge configuration of YOLOv5 to produce "pseudo ground truth" labels of three object categories used in the evaluation, namely: person, bicycle, and vehicle. Motorcycles and human-powered bicycles are merged into class bicycle. Trucks, cars, and buses are merged into class vehicle.

3) Perception module: The Canvas-based scheduling framework imposes no constraint on the perception model. We choose the "large" configuration of YOLOv5 3 , pre-trained on the COCO [11] dataset, as the inference model for object detection. We profile the inference latency with different input sizes and batch sizes in advance on the hardware platform.

4) Canvas Size: Based on the profiling results, we choose an operating frame rate of r = 20Hz. We select a canvas size V GP U of 512 × 512, which is the largest size that can finish execution on the GPU within the frame inter-arrival interval we chose. We further set the maximum object size, v max , to 0.25V GP U , or 256 × 256. Note that, according to Theorem 2, this leads to a utilization bound of 75%. We 3 https://github.com/ultralytics/yolov5 quantize side length into four values, namely 32, 64, 128, and 256. They reasonably cover the dimensions of the common objects present in our video clips. We manually change the frame rate of the input videos to 20Hz to simulate surveillance cameras running at this configuration.

5) Evaluation Metrics: We consider the detection and classification accuracy as a metric for the overall performance of the system, and the deadline miss rate to evaluate the scheduling performance. We compute the mean average precision (mAP) as a way to capture both detection accuracy and classification performance. In addition to comparing the mAP of all object classes, we also consider the average precision of individual classes to get more detailed insights. Thus, to summarize, we use:
• Mean Average Precision: The average precision of all object classes. • Average Precision: The average precision for each object class.
• Deadline Miss Rate: The average deadline miss rate. It evaluates how often an object is not processed within its inspection interval.

div.head: B. Testing Empirical Validity of the Bound
div.p: We start the evaluation by empirically testing the validity of the bound (and indeed the correctness of our implementation). In this experiment, we check if any object inspection deadlines were missed for any of the video clips and record the instantaneous canvas utilization at the time of the deadline miss. We observe no deadline misses when instantaneous canvas utilization (computed for objects in the frame) does not exceed the utilization bound derived in this paper.

Figure 5 shows the relation between instantaneous canvas utilization, as defined in Equation ( 1), and deadline misses. For purposes of plotting the results, we segment the instantaneous utilization into 1% increments on the x-axis and plot on the y-axis the fraction of frames that suffer deadline misses at the corresponding instantaneous utilization value. The plot is not very smooth because it corresponds to statistics of actual frames encountered in our video clips, as opposed to a smooth and systematic exploration of workloads with gradually varied utilization values. A frame is said to have suffered a deadline miss if it coincided with the end of an inspection interval of an object that did not get processed. Note that, for some frames, the utilization as computed from Equation ( 1) was over 100%. As seen in Figure 5, no deadline misses were found up to a utilization ratio of 75%. Starting from 75%+, some deadline misses were observed. Higher utilization values corresponded to more deadline misses. The results coincide exactly with predictions from Theorem 2 that state that the utilization bound is 1 -v max /V GP U . Recall, from Section V-A4 that v max /V GP U in our experimental setup was 0.25, leading to a bound of 75%. While the figure confirms that the bound is tight (note that some deadline misses are observed right around 75%), it also reveals that such deadline misses are unlikely until the utilization reaches closer to 85% (at which point the misses surge).

div.head: C. Evaluation of Scheduling Policies
div.p: 1) Compared Algorithms: Next, we evaluate the efficacy of canvas-based scheduling when combined with multi-frequency object inspection, as described in this paper. We compare two canvas-based scheduling algorithms and two baselines: a) Canvas-EDF: This is the vanilla canvas-based attention scheduling algorithm (with multi-frequency object inspection). This algorithm fills canvas frames with available objects strictly following the earliest deadline first (EDF) policy. Thus, objects are ordered according to EDF and considered in that order for placement in the current canvas frame. Once an object fails to fit in the current frame, the frame is closed (and sent to the GPU). All remaining objects are postponed until a future frame.

b) Canvas-Switching: This algorithm constitutes an optimization of the above. It fills the canvas frames with available objects following the EDF policy, as above. However, even after an object fails to fit in the current frame, subsequent objects are still considered for inclusion in the current frame (in EDF order) until no objects remain for consideration. At that point, the current frame is closed (and sent to the GPU). The remaining objects wait for a future frame. This enhancement allows some smaller objects with later deadlines to be opportunistically included in the current frame, even if a bigger object with an earlier deadline failed to fit because of its size. Note that, at no time (in this algorithm) is an object with a later deadline included in a frame at the expense of an object with an earlier deadline. Rather, objects with later deadlines are merely included opportunistically in gaps left by objects with smaller deadlines in the current frame. c) Batching: It batches objects together and pads them to the same size. The side lengths of objects are quantized into 4 levels: 32, 64, 128, and 256, with 1:1, 1:2, and 2:1 aspect ratios allowed. The scheduler follows an EDF policy to select objects. At the frame rate we consider (20Hz), executing more than 1 batch will exceed the time constraint. As a result, all selected objects must be padded to the same size and processed in one batch. The scheduler iteratively selects objects until the execution time reaches the time limit. d) DS: This baseline downsizes input frames so that they can be processed in real-time. All areas on the frames are uniformly downsized and processed together all at once.

div.head: 2) Policy Evaluation Results:
div.p: The overall accuracy results, reflected by the mean average precision (mAP), are shown in Figure 3. Both Canvas-EDF and Canvas-Switching outperform the other two baseline algorithms. Due to the smaller processing capacity of the batching-based method (partly because of the need to pad some objects to the size of other bigger ones), its accuracy is lower than that of the canvas-based scheduling algorithms. DS has the lowest accuracy because uniformly reducing the entire frames results in information loss for smaller objects and thus affects the detection accuracy. While the batching-based scheduling algorithm cannot process as much frame area as DS, it achieves higher accuracy. The reason is attributed to its ability to allocate the limited computing capacity to the most important regions and utilize the temporal redundancy between frames to skip processing some objects.

To obtain more insights into the performance of compared algorithms, we compare the per-class accuracy for all three considered object classes. The results are shown in Figure 4. DS perform much worse for the classes people and bicycle, as these objects are mostly smaller in size, so they lose too much essential information. In comparison, DS maintains the accuracy of the vehicle class close to that of the two canvasbased scheduling algorithms. This is because vehicles are usually large in size and thus retain enough visual information for detection even after being downsized. The batching-based scheduling algorithm does not perform as well as the canvasbased scheduling algorithms because of its lower processing capacity. Nevertheless, it performs better than DS for the classes people and bicycle. This indicates that for larger objects, downsizing is a good way to trade off accuracy for computing load, whereas for smaller objects, maintaining their original sizes and skipping processing by leveraging temporal redundancy is a better choice.

Finally, we compare the deadline miss rates, defined as the proportion of objects that are not processed within their freshness interval, with the results shown in Table I. Technically, if the properties of objects in the environment are such that the derived utilization bound is never exceeded, there can be no deadline misses. However, as we see from Figure 5, the dataset in question does exceed the utilization bound in many cases. One possibility could be to resize objects until the utilization bound is maintained. Instead, in this experiment, we use the original sizes and simply count the deadline misses. For DS, since the entire frames are downsized until they can be processed at the chosen frame rate, the deadline miss rate is 0. Among the attention scheduling algorithms, both Canvas-EDF and Canvas-Switching achieve very low deadline miss rates, indicating that the processing capacity of the canvas-based attention scheduling algorithms is sufficient for the tested application. On the other hand, the batchingbased scheduling algorithm has a significantly larger number of deadline misses, because of the much smaller processing capacity. Compared with Canvas-EDF, Canvas-Switching has a slightly lower deadline miss rate thanks to the improved canvas utilization achieved with the switching optimization.

div.head: D. A Note on Canvas-based Processing versus Batching
div.p: To explain why canvas-based processing outperforms batching, it is helpful to consider a single numeric example. Before canvas-based processing was introduced, task batching was a standard method commonly used to improve GPU utilization, and has been proven to reduce total execution times. However, it requires that all the regions be of the same size, which limits the flexibility of the execution schedule. When there are regions of multiple size levels, they have to be either padded or resized to the same size otherwise they have to be submitted to the GPU separately. In contrast, with canvasbased execution, all the candidate regions with any size can be submitted together as one GPU request, as long as they can be packed into the canvas frame.

For each target image size, there exist a largest number of regions that can be batched together and finish execution within the frame interval, called the batching limit. We profile it by recording the inference latency for inputs with different batch sizes for each image size. At this batch size, the execution efficiency is the highest for the given image size. The batching limits for target sizes including 32 × 32, 64 × 64, 128 × 128 and 256 × 256 with a frame interval of 50ms are shown in Table II, together with the maximum number of objects of these sizes that can fit into a canvas frame. Only when the batched image size is at 256 × 256, a batch of 4 images has a total area equivalent to a 512 × 512 canvas. At other sizes, even at the batching limit, the most efficient batch size, batching is only able to process a far smaller amount of images compared with canvas-based execution.

We further use a camera frame from the dataset as an example to demonstrate the superiority of canvas-based pro- cessing, illustrated in Figure 7. In this camera frame, there are 6 cars and one person. With batching, they are quantized to 1 256 × 256, 4 128 × 128, and 2 64 × 64 images. Regions of each size are submitted to the GPU separately as a batch, resulting in a total execution time of 97ms, exceeding the frame interval. In comparison, all these objects can be placed into one single canvas frame and be processed by the GPU all at once, taking only 43ms. A large portion of the canvas area is still unused and can further take in additional objects.

div.head: E. Framework Overhead
div.p: We report the latency overhead breakdown of our framework, as shown in Figure 6. The preprocessing steps include object tracking, new region detection, and canvas construction. The postprocessing steps filter and map the detection results to the original frame. The background subtraction and optical flow algorithms, scheduling, preprocessing, and postprocessing steps run on separate CPU processes and therefore pose no overhead on the inference model running on the GPU.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: A growing number of cyber-physical systems (CPS) applications involve executing deep neural network models for the inference subsystem. These applications, such as autonomous driving, require predictable real-time performance on resource-constrained hardware. Previous work addressed this problem from different perspectives. Extensive profiling has been done to understand the underlying scheduling policies of the hardware platforms [12]- [15]. Attention has also been paid to optimizing deep learning frameworks for realtime applications [4], [16]- [19]. Other work aimed to enable Attention Scheduling [2] was proposed in real-time systems literature to tackle the priority-inversion problem commonly found in early perception pipelines. Prior to its introduction, incoming data frames would typically be processed in a first-come-first-served manner. The more important and less important portions of input data were in essence processed together at the the same priority. Thus, computing resources such as GPUs needed to be over-provisioned to process entire frames at the desired frequency. In reality, the areas that required processing would usually constitute a small fraction of any one frame, motivating canvas-based attention scheduling. In general, there are three degrees of freedom for the attention scheduler to trade off between inference performance and resource consumption: spatial [2], [26], temporal [1], and quality [9], [20], [27]- [30]. In order to produce more interpretable schedulability results in this paper, our scheduler does not explicitly manipulate the more subjective dimension of quality (e.g., does not resize the input resolution, except to fit within maximum size constraints). Instead, we focus on spatial and temporal dimensions only.

Work that used the idea of consolidating patches of interest from a large frame into a smaller one (i.e., canvas-based attention scheduling) dates back to 2017 [3]. Our paper is the first to derive a utilization bound for this scheduling framework. A predecessor to canvas-based attention scheduling is to batch the patches of interest together and send them to a parallel processing resource, such as GPU [2], [9], [29]. Batching is known to improve parallelism by grouping tasks together to better utilize the available GPU capacity. However, on lowerend GPUs, it usually requires the individual batched inputs to be of the same size, so that the same processing kernels can be used on all GPU cores. Inputs of different sizes have to be padded, resized, or submitted to the GPU in sequence. Canvas-based processing, in contrast, packs such inputs into one single canvas frame that can be processed as one unit by the GPU, regardless of individual patch sizes, thereby allowing for more flexibility and leading to better optimization.

Finally, the example application implemented in this paper, object detection in videos, has been previously studied in other contexts. Most works assumed access to a powerful cloud server and tried to reduce the communication demand. Various frame filtering approaches were proposed to reduce the number of frames transmitted [31]- [33]. Apart from frame filtering, salience-aware transmission was proposed to reduce the quality of data transmission while not affecting inference results [34]- [37]. Our work, in contrast, not only improves accuracy but also guarantees timely response from the inference subsystem, as long as the bound holds.

VII. DISCUSSION The work presented in this paper has several limitations. The most obvious limitation is perhaps the assumption on the quantization of object sizes. While this assumption was introduced for pragmatic reasons, a direction of future work could be to understand the implications of relaxing this assumption. The schedulability bound derived in this paper was for the EDF scheduling policy. We have not shown that EDF is optimal. Thus, the topic remains open to the derivation of better capacity results. The evaluation section in this paper used a video surveillance dataset. Since the surveillance cameras in this dataset were static, a simple subtraction of two consecutive frames directly revealed all moving objects. In applications where the camera is mounted on a moving platform (e.g., in drones and autonomous cars), an approach relying on optical flow [1] can be used instead. The current paper assumed that objects in the original input are not resized when put into canvas frames (except when they are bigger than the maximum allowable size). Additional trade-offs can be investigated if resizing (specifically, downsizing) was allowed. Finally, we assumed that object inspection tasks have deadlines at the beginning of the next invocation of the task. The schedulability properties of alternative models are delegated to future work.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We described a canvas-based attention scheduling framework and derived a schedulability bound that relates the spatiotemporal properties of regions in the data input to the ability of the scheduler to meet deadlines. The framework is not only more efficient but makes it possible to quantitatively estimate the required computing capacity for guaranteed performance under the expected workload. We implemented the proposed framework for an example object detection application and demonstrated improved efficiency over previous batchingbased approaches with evaluation on a real-world video dataset and the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier platform.
